About: Series LCR — Where the Two Reactances Cancel

Source

Topic
Alternating current — Series RLC circuit, resonance and phase.
Concept
At one drive frequency the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel exactly; the impedance collapses to R and the phase angle passes through zero, changing sign.
Serves
Reading a phasor diagram, distinguishing capacitive/inductive behaviour, understanding resonance and Q for JEE-level AC.
Inquiry
As frequency sweeps up through resonance, does the phase angle grow steadily or change sign?
Misconception
"At resonance the reactances disappear." They are as large as ever — X_L and X_C are both big at ω₀ — but they are equal and opposite, so their phasors cancel and only R is left.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Look at the phasors

V_R points along the current. V_L is a quarter turn ahead of it. V_C is a quarter turn behind. The three arrows rotate together at the drive frequency ω. The green resultant V_net is their vector sum — its angle relative to V_R is the phase φ by which the current lags the applied voltage.

In the right-hand panel the impedance |Z| is plotted against drive frequency ω. A marker sits on the curve at the frequency you set with the ω slider.

2 · Predict — sweep ω up through resonance

You are about to drag ω from well below ω₀ to well above it. As you do, what does the phase angle φ do?

3 · Sweep it and watch

Drag the ω slider from low to high. Watch three things at once:

· V_L (pink) grows and V_C (yellow) shrinks as ω rises — reactances change in opposite directions.
· V_net (green) rotates from BELOW V_R (capacitive, leading) up through V_R (in phase) and above (inductive, lagging).
· The marker on the right rides the impedance curve, dipping into a valley when ω hits ω₀ = 1000 rad/s.

4 · The misconception — do the reactances "disappear" at resonance?

Park ω at 1000 rad/s. V_L and V_C are pointing exactly opposite and V_net collapses onto V_R. What is happening to X_L and X_C at that moment?

5 · Now change R

Drop R from 100 Ω toward 20 Ω. The valley gets deeper and narrower — Q rises — and blunts again when you push R back up. But its bottom never moves along the ω-axis: ω₀ = 1/√(LC) depends only on L and C, never on R.

Now read V_L and V_C on the left. At R = 20 Ω each is about 50 V from a 10 V supply — and they still cancel.

01

At a glance

A resistor, an inductor and a capacitor share one alternating supply. The sim draws their three voltages as rotating arrows, called phasors, beside a graph of the impedance against the drive frequency.

What you'll learn

  • How the drive frequency and the resistance set the impedance, the phase and the current.
  • How the phasor diagram and the impedance graph describe the same circuit.
  • What each control and read-out in the sim does.
R, L and C share one loop, so the same current passes through each. The sim fixes L = 0.1 H, C = 10 µF and a 10 V peak drive.

What's on screen

  • Blue arrow: VR, the voltage across the resistor. It points along the current.
  • Pink arrow: VL, across the inductor, drawn a quarter turn ahead of VR.
  • Amber arrow: VC, across the capacitor, drawn a quarter turn behind VR.
  • Green arrow: Vnet, the sum of the three. The green arc between VR and Vnet is the phase angle φ.
  • Impedance graph: the blue curve is |Z| against ω. An amber dot marks the drive frequency and a dashed green line marks ω₀.
  • Read-outs in the side panel. While a guided-inquiry prediction is open, φ, XL, XC and the regime show a dash.

03

The three voltages add as phasors to the drive voltage

One current I runs through R, L and C. VR is in step with I, VL leads it by 90° and VC lags it by 90°, so the last two point in opposite directions. Each is the current times that element's opposition:

VR = I R,   VL = I XL,   VC = I XC,   XL = ωL,   XC = 1/(ωC)
Peak values. Vnet is the vector sum of the three, and its length is I Z, the 10 V drive.

Take ω = 500 rad/s and R = 100 Ω. Then XL = 50 Ω, XC = 200 Ω and Z = √(100² + 150²) = 180.3 Ω, so I = 10/180.3 = 55.5 mA. The voltages are VR = 5.55 V, VL = 2.77 V and VC = 11.09 V.

VL and VC partly cancel, leaving 11.09 − 2.77 = 8.32 V. Then √(5.55² + 8.32²) = 10.0 V, the drive. Vnet stays at 10 V at every setting, even when VC alone is larger.

See itSet ω = 500 rad/s with R = 100 Ω. Watch for: VC = 11.1 V as the longest arrow, VR = 5.5 V, VL = 2.8 V, and Vnet = 10.0 V.
04

The phase changes sign as ω passes ω₀

The phase angle φ is the angle between Vnet, the drive, and VR, which has the phase of the current. The triangle of R and the net reactance gives it:

Z = √(R² + (XL − XC)²),   tan φ = (XL − XC) / R
φ is negative when XC is larger and positive when XL is larger.

At low ω the capacitor wins, because XC = 1/(ωC) is large. The net reactance is negative, so φ is negative. The regime is capacitive and the current leads the drive. At ω = 500 rad/s, tan φ = −150/100, so φ = −56.3°.

At high ω the inductor wins and φ turns positive. The current lags. At ω = 2000 rad/s the net reactance is +150 Ω and φ = +56.3°. Z is again 180.3 Ω, so Z alone cannot tell the two sides apart. The sign of φ can.

See itSet ω = 500 rad/s with R = 100 Ω. Watch for: φ = −56.3° and the regime capacitive (lead).
See itRaise ω to 2000 rad/s. Watch for: the same Z = 180.3 Ω, but φ = +56.3°, VL = 11.1 V, and the regime inductive (lag).
05

At ω₀ the reactances are large and equal, so they cancel

Setting XL = XC gives ω²LC = 1, the resonant frequency:

ω0 = 1/√(LC),   XL = XC at ω0
For L = 0.1 H and C = 10 µF: ω₀ = 1/√(0.1 × 10⁻⁵) = 1000 rad/s.

At ω₀ each reactance is XL = XC = 100 Ω, large and not zero. They are equal, and VL and VC point in opposite directions. They cancel as vectors, the net reactance is 0, and Z = R = 100 Ω with φ = 0.

The current is then at its largest, I = 10/100 = 0.1 A. Each voltage is 0.1 × 100 = 10 V, so VR = VL = VC = 10 V. The dashed line for VL + VC shrinks to a point, and Vnet lies right on VR.

See itSet ω = 1000 rad/s with R = 100 Ω. Watch for: XL = XC = 100 Ω, φ = 0.0°, and VL and VC as opposite arrows of equal length.
06

The valley of |Z| marks the peak of the current

The drive is fixed, so the peak current is I = 10/Z. Z is smallest where the reactances cancel, so the current is largest there, and it falls away on both sides.

The table is for R = 100 Ω. On the linear ω axis the valley looks lopsided. It is even in ratio: two frequencies give the same Z when ω1ω2 = ω₀². Here 500 × 2000 = 1000², so both have Z = 180.3 Ω.

See itSet ω = 700 rad/s with R = 100 Ω. Watch for: the amber dot on the left slope, labelled |Z| = 123.7 Ω.
See itSet ω = 2000 rad/s. Watch for: the dot on the right slope at |Z| = 180.3 Ω, the same height as at 500.
07

Q sets the sharpness of the valley, and R sets Q

The quality factor compares the reactance at resonance with the resistance. At ω₀ the reactive voltages are Q times the drive:

Q = ω0L / R,   VL = VC = Q V,   Δω = R / L
Δω is the width between the half-power points, where Z = R√2. Q = ω₀/Δω.

R does not enter ω₀, so the valley stays centred at 1000 rad/s while its width changes. A small R gives a large Q, a tall peak of current and a narrow band. A large R gives a small Q and a broad, shallow valley.

R (Ω)QI at ω₀ (A)VL = VC (V)Δω (rad/s)
205.000.50050.0200
502.000.20020.0500
1001.000.10010.01000
3000.330.0333.33000

At R = 20 Ω the half-power points are at 905 and 1105 rad/s, where Z = 28.3 Ω. The reactive arrows reach 50 V against a 10 V drive. They are drawn to the rim of the panel and labelled with their true value.

See itSet ω = 1000 rad/s and lower R to 20 Ω. Watch for: Q = 5.00, Z = 20.0 Ω, VL and VC labelled 50.0 V, and a narrow valley.
See itKeep ω = 1000 rad/s and raise R to 300 Ω. Watch for: Q = 0.33, Z = 300.0 Ω, VL = VC = 3.3 V, and the dashed ω₀ line unmoved.
08

Where it matters

  • Radio tuning. A tuner is an LC circuit whose ω₀ is set to a station's frequency. At ω₀ the station drives a large current, and other frequencies meet a larger Z.
  • Selectivity. A high Q gives a narrow band, so nearby stations are rejected. Too high a Q cuts into the band that one station needs, so the choice of R balances the two.
  • Component ratings. At resonance L and C each carry Q times the drive voltage. A coil and capacitor in a high-Q circuit need insulation rated for that, not for the supply.
09

Summary

In one line. In a series LCR circuit, the drive frequency sets both reactances, and with R they fix the impedance, the phase and the current.

Key points

  • XL = ωL, XC = 1/(ωC), Z = √(R² + (XL − XC)²) and tan φ = (XL − XC)/R.
  • φ is negative below ω₀ (capacitive, current leads) and positive above it (inductive, current lags).
  • At ω₀ = 1/√(LC), Z = R and the current peaks. Q = ω₀L/R and Δω = R/L.

Common mix-ups

  • "At resonance both reactances are zero." Each is 100 Ω here. Only their difference is zero.
  • "A smaller R moves the resonance." ω₀ = 1/√(LC) does not contain R. R changes Q and the width of the valley.
  • "No element can have more voltage than the drive." The voltages are out of step, so VL or VC alone can be larger. At R = 20 Ω each is 50 V.

Things to try on your own

  • At ω = 1500 rad/s with R = 100 Ω, find Z and φ. Z = 130.2 Ω and φ = +39.8°.
  • At ω = 700 rad/s with R = 100 Ω, find VC. It is 11.55 V.
  • At ω₀ with R = 50 Ω, find Q and VL. Q = 2.00 and VL = 20 V.
